Cross-references on p.28 point to ch.2 sec.2.3 [Reduplications] and sec.2.4 [Prefixes] (part, images pp.11 and 13); scan, the verification and the verification each re-rendered image p.22 (thesis p.28) with page render at 220 dpi and read it as a; the verification also read images 1, 17, 18.
catalog_quote: [p.7] Any syllable that is followed by a juncture /'/ (clause-bounding and topic-succeeding juncture) or /#/ (sentence-bounding juncture) is phonetically characterized as a major syllable (cf. 1.5.). A major syllable carries complete phonetic features. Syllables that are not major syllables are minor syllables. ... Minor syllables are, as a principle, pronounced medium or weak in stress, less distinctive in tone and medium or short in duration in normal speech. [p.23] In a syntactic unit composed of more than two morphemes, only the final syllable is realized with its complete segmental and supra-segmental features (viz. major syllable), while a syllable in a non-final position is equipped with more or less vague and weakened sort of tonal and other phonetic features (viz. minor syllable). [p.24] The analysis of other types of supra-segmental features like intonation, stress etc. is not attempted here. [p.28] Minor syllables in general are pronounced medium or short in duration, and medium or weak in stress in normal speech as already pointed out. Especially, those in reduplications (cf. 2.3.) and in prefixed lexemes (cf. 2.4.) are pronounced in such a reduced manner that they are marked with a small-cased 0 on the upper-right side of the form. The Lachi language is similar to Burmese than to Chinese in that its stress-placing tendency is of rear-ward nature rather than of forward (cf. application of tone 0 in the first syllable in a reduplicated lexeme).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Lachi is a tone language (six-plus tones incl. a reduced 'tone 0') with right-edge prominence: within a lexeme or syntactic unit only the final syllable (the 'major syllable', i.e. the one before a juncture) is realised with full stress, full tone and full length; all preceding 'minor' syllables — prefixes, first members of reduplications, non-final morphemes of compounds/expressions — are medium-to-weak in stress, tonally vague (often tone 0) and shortened, i.e. an iambic/final-prominence pattern. The author states (p.23) that 'only the final syllable is realized with its complete segmental and supra-segmental features' and that a separate analysis of stress and intonation 'is not attempted here'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described; minor syllables are graded only as 'medium or weak' in stress, with prefixes and reduplicant first syllables the most reduced (marked tone 0).
new_statements.exceptions: Tonal contrasts can survive on minor syllables in some minimal pairs (e.g. /m⁰ qhe⁴³/ 'day before yesterday' vs /m²³ qhe⁴³/ 'meal', p.9); tone values of free morphemes in minor position fluctuate with speech style; sporadic Vietnamese loans take an exceptional 44 tone; tone sandhi triggered by reduced rising-tone minor syllables raises the following tone to 45 (sec.1.7).
new_statements.domain_note: Major/minor status is defined relative to juncture (clause/sentence boundary), so the primary domain is the syntactic unit/phrase in connected speech; at word level, prefixed lexemes and reduplications have a reduced first syllable and full final syllable; monosyllabic citation forms are major syllables. Variety: Tân Lợi hamlet (Bắc Quang, Hà Giang), speakers originating from Bản Phùng (Southern/Long-haired Lachi).
new_statements.identity_note: Kosaka 2000 describes the Lachi of Tân Lợi hamlet (Bắc Quang district, Hà Giang, Vietnam), a secondary settlement of speakers from Bản Phùng (Hoàng Su Phì); main informant born 1946 in Bản Phùng. This is Ostapirat's 'Southern Lachi' (Long-haired Lachi), within Glottolog lach1248 / ISO lbt (not White Lachi lwh of Bản Pang). Li Yunbing 2000 and Liang Min describe Flowery Lachi of Jinchang, Maguan (China), the Northern variety of the same language.
